before:
Manaus's airport, 14 km north of downtown, run by Vinci Airports, and a more interesting building than most.

The name has a story. It was designed to handle Concorde and was originally called the Supersonic Airport of Manaus, a name it lost in December 1973 while still being built, in favour of Air Marshal Eduardo Gomes.

It opened in March 1976, replacing Ponta Pelada, which became the Manaus Air Force Base. At the time it was the most modern airport in Brazil and the first in the country with jet bridges.

Terminal 1 handles all domestic and international passengers, and Terminal 2, from 1985, takes general aviation. Freight matters a great deal here: three cargo terminals covering 49,000 square metres can process up to 12,000 tonnes a month, two of them handling exports and one imports.

The airport was enlarged again ahead of the 2014 World Cup, when Manaus was a host city. An Infraero assessment in 2011 put it in good shape, running at less than 70 per cent of capacity.
after:
Manaus's airport, north of the city centre, run by Vinci Airports.

The name has a story. It was originally called the Supersonic Airport of Manaus, a name it lost in December 1973 in favour of Air Marshal Eduardo Gomes.

Opened in March 1976, it replaced Ponta Pelada, which became the Manaus Air Force Base.

Freight matters a great deal here, and the airport says its cargo terminal is the third largest in Brazil.

claims.claim: north of the city centre
claims.note: Was '14 km north of downtown'. The coordinates give 7.6 km in a straight line at 339 degrees (north); 14 km is a ratio of 1.85, outside the tolerance, and no written source other than Wikipedia gives a distance, so the figure is cut and only the direction kept. The operator places the airport in the Tarumã district of Manaus's west zone (zona oeste), which is the city's administrative zone, not a compass bearing from the centre.
